segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth. Do you remember your first day at school, Neil?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Yes, I do. I changed schools quite a lot when I was a kid, so I had lots of first days and they were never easy. How about you, Beth?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Well, my mum always tells this story about how I was crying a lot on my first day,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: but apparently as soon as she left I was quite happy.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So my mum spent the day being a bit sad and I was completely fine.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, yes, starting school and making new friends is difficult for many children,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: but it's not just the kids who find it challenging.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: For mums and dads who drop their kids off at the school gates in the morning

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and pick them up again at the end of the school day,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: making friends with other mums can be just as hard.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here, BBC presenter Nuala McGovern discusses this problem using the term mum friends.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So if you are a mum dropping off or picking up the kids this week,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: how do you feel about hanging out with other mum friends?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I find that term kind of interesting as well.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Mum friends. They're never called friends, they're called mum friends.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Do you struggle to make those relationships or do you thrive on them or are you perfectly happy without them?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Mum friends are usually the mums of other children in your child class at school They might go for coffee together help out with babysitting or chat about being a mother But is making

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: new mum friends really the positive experience it's often described as, or an additional

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: stress for already overworked mothers? That's what we'll be discussing in this programme

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: along with some useful new vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: if the idea of mum friends is new to you, why not take a minute to read through the list of

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: vocabulary before you listen? It's easy to find on our website,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Now Beth, I have a question for you. Another term often associated with mum friends is playdate,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: a time that parents arrange for their children to play together. But according to the Oxford

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: English Dictionary, where does the term playdate come from? Is the origin in A. Australia, B. New

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Zealand or C. the United States of America?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I'm going to guess the USA. C.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK. Feeling confident?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, we'll see at the end of the programme.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: For some mums, dropping their kids off at school reminds them of when they themselves were little

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and under pressure to make friends. Listen as mum Jane Charrington-Cook describes

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: these feelings to BBC Radio 4 programme Woman's Hour.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The school gates take you back to being back at school. It is like you said, a high school

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: clique. You've got the sporty mums over there, you've got the glam mums over there, you've

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: got you know and if you don fit into one of those it really really difficult to navigate And yet you all there just because your children were born in the same year It a really weird thing

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Jane says that mums often form cliques, small groups of people who like spending time together and seem unfriendly towards others.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: For example, at Jane's daughter's school, there's a clique of sporty mums and a clique of glam mums who put on makeup and dress up.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Jane uses the adjective glam as a shortened form of the word glamour, meaning attractive and exciting.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Problems start when someone doesn't fit into one of the cliques.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If you fit into a group of people, you feel you belong and are accepted, probably because you are similar to them.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So, some mums feel rejected from cliques and worry about their children being left out of playdates.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But other mums don't mind. If people want to be friends, that's fine. And if they don't, that's fine too.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Being a mum is hard enough without adding more stress.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Jane definitely belongs to this group, as she explains to BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I think I'd had some really bad experiences at baby groups,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: where you're trying to make your child do yoga or paint when they're four months old,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and trying to bond with these other women, and I just thought this is ridiculous.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I pretty much straight away realised it was going to be just down to luck if I met somebody that I clicked with.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Jane says it down to luck if she makes mum friends If you say something is down to luck you mean it depends on chance rather than any skill or effort you make But there always the possibility you meet someone and click with them become friends as soon as you start talking

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Well, I know something that isn't down to luck, Neil the answer to your question.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Ah yes, I asked you about the origin of the term playdate. Which country does it come from?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I think it's the USA.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, Beth, you are right. So, well done.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: According to the Oxford English Dictionary, playdate was first used in the Lincoln Daily Star newspaper in Nebraska, USA in 1915.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt starting with playdate, an arrangement that parents make for their young children to play together.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A clique is a small group of people who spend a lot of time together and may seem unfriendly towards other people.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Glam is short for glamorous, meaning visually attractive and exciting.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If you fit into a group of people, you belong and feel accepted by them because you're similar to them.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If you say something is down to luck, you mean that it depends on chance or luck, rather than any skill or effort you make.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And finally, if you click with someone, you feel a friendly and positive connection when you meet them for the first time.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Once again, our time is up. Why not head over to the BBC Learning English website to find a quiz and worksheet for this programme while it's still fresh in your mind. See you again soon. Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Bye.
